name: Daphne Oram
hook: The BBC studio manager who fought to open the Radiophonic Workshop, then left within a year to build her own studio and her own machine.

blurb.age7: A woman who worked at the BBC and made strange sounds with tape. She helped start the BBC's special sound studio.
blurb.age13: Daphne Oram worked as a sound engineer at the BBC. In 1957 she made the sounds for a radio play called Private Dreams and Public Nightmares, cut together from tape. The next year the BBC opened the Radiophonic Workshop, with Oram running it. She left in January 1959 because the BBC wouldn't let her make music, only sound effects. At home in Kent she built the Oramics machine, which turned drawings on film into sound.
blurb.adult: Oram's departure is the reason the Workshop's most famous piece is Derbyshire's, not hers. Her own studio at Tower Folly in Kent and the Oramics machine, drawn sound on 35mm film, were years ahead of commercial synthesis and were funded largely by her own commissions and a Gulbenkian grant. Two strokes in the 1990s ended her working life. The end year is her death in 2003, since the date she stopped working isn't pinned down. The home town given is her birthplace in Wiltshire.

signatureTracks.title: Private Dreams and Public Nightmares
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: Made with the writer Frederick Bradnum. A radio piece built from treated tape, and the argument for the Workshop's existence.

signatureTracks.title: Still Point
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: Written for orchestra, turntables and live electronics. It was refused and not performed until 2016, which says a lot about her career.
